content: The gastrointestinal system of preterm infants is functionally immature, which makes them prone to feeding intolerance. Erythromycin, a motilin receptor agonist, has a prokinetic effect by stimulating contractile activity during the interdigestive phase of gastrointestinal motility. This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of erythromycin in preventing and treating feeding intolerance in preterm infants. A systematic review of the literature was conducted using the Cochrane Neonatal Collaborative Review Group's search strategy. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving erythromycin to enhance gastrointestinal motility in preterm infants were identified from multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, covering publications up to December 2007. Additional sources included cross-references, abstracts, and manual journal searches. Initially, the review focused on studies using erythromycin at doses of 3 to 12 mg/kg/day in preterm infants born at less than 36 weeks of gestation who exhibited feeding intolerance. However, a significant number of studies utilized higher doses of erythromycin (>12 mg/kg/day) or administered it prophylactically to infants at risk of feeding intolerance. Consequently, a post hoc decision was made to include these studies in the review. The studies were divided into two categories: prevention and treatment. Data from each category were analyzed separately. Subgroup analyses were performed within each category based on low-dose (3 to 12 mg/kg/day) and high-dose (>12 mg/kg/day) erythromycin administration. The primary outcome measured was the time required to achieve full enteral feeding. Secondary outcomes included adverse effects of erythromycin, duration of total parenteral nutrition (TPN), weight gain, incidence of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), and length of hospital stay. A total of ten RCTs were included in the review, comprising three prevention studies and seven treatment studies. The studies exhibited significant variability in their definitions of feeding intolerance, as well as in the measurement, analysis, and reporting of outcomes. This heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis for most outcomes. However, it was noted that studies using higher treatment doses of erythromycin (40 to 50 mg/kg/day) or involving infants older than 32 weeks of gestational age reported more favorable effects in improving feeding intolerance. Meta-analysis of high-dose prevention studies revealed no statistically significant reduction in the incidence of NEC (relative risk [RR] 0.59, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.11 to 3.01; risk difference [RD] -0.021, 95% CI -0.087 to 0.045). Similarly, meta-analysis of high-dose treatment studies showed no significant difference in the incidence of septicemia (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.45; RD -0.04, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.08). The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to recommend the use of erythromycin, either at low or high doses, for preterm infants with or at risk of feeding intolerance. Further research is necessary to determine whether a specific dose range of erythromycin might be effective as a prokinetic agent, particularly in preterm infants older than 32 weeks of gestational age.
